extracted_by: hand, T-0292 — the Democrat read, October 1834
note: Vol. I No. 47. The issue that carries the post-office list of letters remaining at Chicago on 1 October 1834 in its best surviving state, on page 1 — 175 names read at name level. Beside it on page 1 the standing October advertisements: the Democrat's own office offered for sale at the corner of Clark and South Water streets, the Eagle Hotel changing hands, G. Blanshard's houses and his lot at Randolph and Wells, and John H. Kinzie's 20-by-45-foot store in Kinzie's Addition. On page 3 the town's SECOND fire ordinance of the month, passed at the Tremont House on 11 October, which arms the Fire Wardens appointed on 20 September with the power to summon bystanders into a bucket line and puts a numbered badge on them.

claims.normalized: List of Letters REMAINING in the Post Office at Chicago, Ill. Oct. 1, 1834. — set in two sub-columns of names running down the printed column. The right-hand sub-column reads continuously from Lilley to Woodruff and is transcribed above; the left-hand sub-column, which carries the alphabet from A to about H, is cut down its left edge by the segmenter's crop and survives only in fragments ([…] on most rows). Six of its rows are legible whole and are named here — Benson, John H.; Bowen, Erastus; Bowen, Albert W.; Brown, Jas.; Hancock, Harry [B.]; Hopkins, Hannah — and the rest are recorded as absent rather than guessed at.
claims.notes: THE POST-OFFICE LETTER LIST OF 1 OCTOBER 1834, AND THE CENSUS PROXY THE EPIC'S RULING 1 ASKS FOR. This is the third of three insertions of the same list — it also stands in 1834-10-08 (page 3, columns 1-2) and 1834-10-15 (page 3, columns 3-4) — and this printing is the best witness of the three: 1834-10-08 loses the whole left sub-column and 1834-10-15 splits the list across two segmenter crops. Every name here is `letter_list_only`: a listed name mints a resident candidate and nothing stronger. 118 names are read out of the right-hand sub-column and 6 out of the left. THE LEFT SUB-COLUMN IS THE GAP AND IT IS MEASURED, NOT WAVED AT: it holds about 130 rows of A-to-H surnames, its beginnings survive at the RIGHT EDGE of 1834-10-15 page 3 column 2 (`Andrey`, `Abell`, `Atwate`, `Akers`, `Beilly`, `Bryant`, `Barlow`, `Brooks`, `Bird`…) and its endings at the LEFT EDGE of that issue's column 3 (`we, David`, `ze, Williem`, `t, Jesse`, `ums, William-`…), so the two halves are joinable by sense but not inside one locator, because a claim's quote comes from ONE column. Joining them is a separate reading, and nothing here pretends to have done it. Rows whose OCR gives no readable surname at all — twelve of them in the right sub-column — are left unnamed for the same reason.

claims.notes: A DEALER'S OWN ADDRESS, GIVEN AS A LANDMARK RATHER THAN A NUMBER — 'opposite Dr. Temple's, Lake-st.' — and it is the placement, not the property, that this claim is for. The houses and the corner lot at Randolph and Wells are stock he is selling; where he sits to sell it is Lake Street facing John T. Temple's. Temple is a fixed point all month: his own advertisement of a store house and a dwelling stands two columns away (1834-10-08 page 3 column 2), and 1834-10-15 page 3 column 2 carries a lot 'one lot east of Haddock's Tavern, on Lake strect' — three Lake Street anchors in one month. The dateline is cut to `Ont, 2` and is left as the day the paper printed rather than supplied.

claims.notes: THE DEMOCRAT'S OWN OFFICE, PUT AT A CORNER IN PLAIN WORDS. The issue of 1834-07-02 could only get out 'in the building[ at the] corner of South Water and C…' before the column edge cut it (that issue's claim c028, T-0289); here the same building is named whole — the CORNER OF CLARK AND SOUTH WATER STREETS — because the paper is selling it. It is one building doing two things: W. Kimball's store, and the printing office. That matters downstream, because two 1834 businesses are placed by reference to this building and nothing else: John Watkins's school room 'opposite the Print[ing office]' and J. H. Mulford's store 'one door West of the Printing [office]' (1834-07-09, claims c017 and the one below it). Their anchor now has a corner. The advertisement is dated 8 October and runs unchanged in 1834-10-15 and 1834-10-29, so the sale had not closed by the end of the month; possession was offered from 1 November, which is a date a reconstruction of July 1835 should treat as a change of occupancy it does not yet know the end of.

claims.notes: A TAVERN CHANGES HANDS ON A DATED DAY, and the date is inside the window this project reconstructs. Paul J. Carli gave up the EAGLE HOTEL on 22 September 1834 to J. Shrigley. Three weeks later the house is still being advertised under its old name — 1834-10-15 page 3 column 2 sends a man wanting work to 'application at the Eagte Tavern' — so the sign did not change when the landlord did, which is exactly the kind of thing a reconstruction has to know before it letters a signboard. Ruling 3 reads this as a SUCCESSION and not a closure: the business stands, the proprietor changes, and both men are recorded with their dates. Carli's forename is cut to `P.` in the notice's first line and printed whole at its signature, so the supply is from the same advertisement.

claims.notes: A BUILDING WITH ITS DIMENSIONS PRINTED — twenty feet by forty-five, with a counting room inside that footprint and three further rooms let as offices — which is rare enough in this corpus to be worth a card on its own. It is placed only by ADDITION and not by street: 'Kinzie's Addition' is the north-side subdivision, so this is a north-bank store, and the advertisement's boast that these are 'by far the best finished rooms' in the town is the landlord's, recorded as his and not as fact. The same notice runs in 1834-10-08 and 1834-10-15 without change. Nothing here says which lot, so the placement class is `street_only` with no street to put it on — recorded as `none`, which is the honest value rather than an absence.

claims.normalized: Town Ordinance. [At] a meeting of the President and Trustees [o]f the Town of Chicago, held at the Tre[mont] House in said town, on the [ele]venth day of [October] A.D. 1834:—The following Ordinance [was ad]opted, to wit: [Sect]ion 1. Be it Ordained by th[e] President and [Trustee]s of the town of Chicago, That the Fire [Warde]ns appointed under the Ordinance dated [the twentiet]h day of September A.D. 1834, be, and [they] hereby are authorized, and it is hereby [made their] duty to att[end] at all fires that may [occur] within the limits of the corporation, and [they] are hereby authorised and empowered to [summon] any bystander or bystanders at or near [the fi]re to aid and assist in extinguishing the [same,] whether it be to enter the ranks or lines [forme]d for passing water or buckets, or to aid [in prom]oting such means as to said Wardens [may see]m calculated to carry into effect the [object] of this Ordinance. And the said Wardens [or eith]er of them are hereby empowered to give [such d]irections for the purpose aforesaid, as [they] may seem necessary. Any and all persons [refusing] when summoned and directed [by said] Warden or Wardens as aforesaid with[out go]od and sufficient cause or excuse, shall be [liable to] a fine of five dollars, to be recovered on [complai]nt before any Justice of the Peace or [other] court of competent jurisdiction, in the [same] manner as other fines are by law recovered.
claims.notes: THE BUCKET LINE, ORDERED BY THE TOWN — the second fire ordinance of October 1834 and the one that says what actually happened when a roof caught. The Wardens appointed three weeks earlier (1834-10-01 and 1834-10-08 carry that ordinance; see this month's claims on both) may SUMMON any bystander at or near a fire, and the thing the bystander is summoned into is named: 'the ranks or lines formed for passing water or buckets.' A refusal costs five dollars. For a reconstruction that has to decide what a Chicago street held in 1835, this is the documented answer to where the water came from — hands and buckets, not an engine: no engine, hose, hook or ladder is mentioned anywhere in either ordinance. The meeting place is the TREMONT HOUSE, as it was on 29 September (1834-10-01 page 3 column 1), so the board's room that autumn is a tavern's room. Every supply here closes a word cut at the column's left edge from the sentence it stands in; the ordinance's own date is read `Tiith` and is supplied as the eleventh only because the ordinance takes effect on the twelfth, four lines further down, and is bracketed.

claims.notes: A BADGE ON A HAT WITH A WARD NUMBER ON IT — the only piece of clothing this project has a town ordinance for. Whichever ward the fire is in, that ward's Warden becomes Warden in Chief for the duration and everyone present, other Wardens included, is under his orders. The four wards were drawn on 20 September (see 1834-10-08 page 4 column 4, claim c013 there), so a numbered badge is readable as a place: '1' is east of the centre of Lasalle street, '3' is north of the river. In force from 12 October 1834, which is the same day the September ordinance took effect. THE CLERK'S NAME IS THE WEAKEST READING ON THIS PAGE: it prints as `E. S. W. Coser` and is left `C[hurch]`-shaped only in this note and NOT in the normalized text, where it is bracketed as a supply; the clerk of 30 July was Isaac Harmon (1834-07-30, claim c001) and this one signs pro tem, so no identity is asserted and no person is minted from it.

claims.notes: A TWO-STOREY DWELLING HOUSE WITH A SHOP IN IT, placed against a named house across the street. This is the shape of an 1834 Chicago frontage stated outright: ground floor a store, first floor rooms let for offices or as a family's lodging, the whole thing a DWELLING house rather than a purpose-built store. The anchor, the Exchange Coffee House, is also where the advertiser sits, and it turns up again a week later — the bake shop sold at auction on 29 October stands 'on Lake street, a[bove] the Exchange Coffee House' (1834-10-29 page 3 column 2). Two independent placements on one landmark inside eight days is the kind of chain that eventually puts a building on the ground; neither claim gives a side or a distance, so this placement is `relative` and stays that way.

claims.notes: A TAILORING SHOP OPENS IN THE SCENE WINDOW AND PLACES ITSELF ON THE TREMONT HOUSE. The firm is new this month — the notice is dated the day of the issue — and it is almost certainly the successor to Thomas S. Eels, who advertised alone through the summer with orders left at G. S. Hubbard & Co.'s store (1834-10-08 page 3 column 3, and 1834-07-09). The SIDE OF THE TREMONT HOUSE IS THE ONE THING THIS RUN COULD NOT SETTLE: this printing reads `go die Hrvth ‘ot Tro-` and the reprint a week later reads `«1 eth of Tree nt House` (1834-10-29 page 3 column 2), which is 'north' in the first and 'south' in the second and cannot be both. It is left `[nor]th` with the bracket standing and the disagreement written here, rather than resolved to whichever reads better. The Tremont House is the board of trustees' meeting room in the same month, so this is a shop next door to the town's government.

claims.normalized: $40 Reward. [ST]OLEN last Saturday night from the stable [of the] subscriber living one mile south of [Chica]go, a bright bay Horse, seventeen hands [high,] well made, black mane and tail both heavy, [wh]ite on his legs [as] recollected, a very noted [mark o]n his withers occasioned by the Pistol[s…] [about ten] inches down [h]is [le]ft shoulder, remark[ably high] carriage, a first rate racker and [pacer… Said horse is supposed to have been stolen] by a soldier, a deserter from Fort Dearborn. [$30] reward will be paid for the horse and thief[, and $10 reward] for the horse. JAMES HERRINGTON, JR.
claims.notes: A DESERTER FROM FORT DEARBORN, NAMED AS SUCH IN AN ADVERTISEMENT. The garrison is a fact this reconstruction already carries; a horse thief walking out of it is the garrison behaving like a place people leave. The advertisement also puts a STABLE one mile south of the town in October 1834, which is a structure outside the plat at a stated distance and on no stated road. The word-by-word supplies here are heavy and every one is bracketed; the pistol-mark clause is cut across two lines and its reading is carried further in the reprint at 1834-10-29 page 3 column 2, where the same advertisement runs with different OCR damage. The reward figures are read off that reprint's cleaner `$30 … $10` and are bracketed here.
